results.title: Retail assortment under demand shocks: Evidence from the US yogurt market - Ma - 2024 - Journal of the Agricultural and Applied Economics Association - Wiley Online Library
results.content: Using heterogeneity in timing, location, and magnitude of income and wealth shocks associated with the 2008 Great Recession, we explore how US retail stores adjusted product offerings under local demand shocks. We use NielsenIQ Retail Scanner (retail measurement services [RMS]) data on the US yogurt market to study product portfolios offered by retailers in the period surrounding the sizable shocks on local income and wealth caused by the 2008 Great Recession. We control for a large set of variables to strengthen the baseline identification, including the total number of UPCs available on the market (accounting for manufacturers' responses to aggregate demand shocks), the pre-Recession products offered by the stores (accounting for path dependence), subsidies from food assistance programs (controlling for another key source of local demand shocks), local retail competition, and retailer, market, and time fixed effects. While several studies have theoretically and empirically examined product adding and dropping by manufacturers (Antoniades et al., 2023; Bernard et al., 2010) and the expansion of private labels in retail markets during an economic recession (Dubé et al., 2018), we are one of the first to provide an empirical analysis of product offerings of retail stores under local demand shocks. Facing local income and wealth shocks, retail stores remove yogurt products and reduce varieties, controlling for time-invariant chain and market characteristics, seasonality, and so forth. To identify the impact of demand shocks on the product assortment of retail stores, we take the advantage of rich spatial and temporal variation in county-level income and wealth driven by the 2008 Great Recession (see statistics in Section 2). As long as income and wealth shocks on the local market are independent from product offerings of individual stores, controlling for the set of variables and fixed effects specified in Section 3.1, our identification strategy would work. (5) To confirm that local demand shocks drive assortment in a store, we add retailer-chain-level income and wealth as control variables. To estimate the direct effect of local demand shocks on UPC-level prices, we control for the store-level product offerings. Using scanner data from the US yogurt market, we provide insights into store-level assortment adjustments driven by income and wealth shocks in the local market.

Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply Effects of COVID-19: A Real-time Analysis Consumer Responses to the COVID-19 Crisis: Evidence from Bank Account Transaction Data Production Networks and Epidemic Spreading: How to Restart the UK Economy? * : R Maria Del Río-ChanonaR Maria Del Río-Chanona Sectoral Effects of Social Distancing Macroeconomic Implications of COVID-19: Can Negative Supply Shocks Cause Demand Shortages? ### Supply and demand shocks in the COVID-19 pandemic: An industry and occupation perspective * : R Maria Del Río-ChanonaR Maria Del Río-Chanona We provide quantitative predictions of first order supply and demand shocks for the U.S. economy associated with the COVID-19 pandemic at the level of individual occupations and industries. ### In and out of lockdown: Propagation of supply and demand shocks in a dynamic input-output model * : R Maria Del Río-ChanonaR Maria Del Río-Chanona Economic shocks due to Covid-19 were exceptional in their severity, suddenness and heterogeneity across industries. To study the upstream and downstream propagation of these industry-specific demand and supply shocks, we build a dynamic input-output model inspired by previous work on the economic response to natural disasters.
